[1873] Revision of laws and regulations

[1874] There are a number of regulations that have emergency preparedness as their purpose or that contain provisions with emergency preparedness content

[1875] It is important that the sectors ensure that the emergency preparedness regulations are updated and harmonized with related regulations in other sectors, both to avoid different interpretations and conflicts of priorities, and to ensure effective management and practice of the regulations

[1876] In recent years, the Armed Forces have carried out extensive work on revising and updating emergency preparedness plans and operational planning at various levels for crises and armed conflict

[1877] The armed forces' operational capability depends on support from civilian actors in a number of areas and close cooperation with civilian authorities on crisis management

[1878] Armed conflict in Norway will lead to an extraordinary need for goods and services for the Armed Forces, such as food, transportation, fuel, power, e-communications and sanitation

[1879] These are goods and services that are mostly provided by civilian actors, both public and private

[1880] In order to facilitate the operational capability of the Armed Forces, it is of crucial importance that the Armed Forces describe their needs to ensure that the civilian side is able to deliver the necessary support to the Armed Forces

[1881] This work is underway in several areas, including health preparedness, fuel supply, transport infrastructure, transport services and transport resources

[1882] Civilian and military total defence actors should actively contribute to each other's planning processes, at both local, regional and national levels, in order to establish a mutual understanding of each other's needs, capacities and ability to support each other

[1883] The National Emergency Response System (NBS) is a cross-sectoral procedural and decision-making tool for central political authorities and individual agency heads in the event of a security crisis, armed conflict and other cross-sectoral crises caused by serious, intentional acts

[1884] NBS is harmonized with NATO's emergency preparedness system, NATO's Crisis Response System (NCRS), to ensure rapid and coordinated decisions between Norway and NATO, but is adapted to national conditions and needs

[1885] The NBS consists of the Defence Sector Emergency Preparedness System (BFF) and the Civil Emergency Preparedness System (SBS

[1886] All sectors on the civil side have a responsibility associated with NBS

[1887] The Ministry of Justice and Public Security is responsible for coordinating SBS on the civilian side, while the Ministry of Defence is responsible for coordinating BFF in the defence sector

[1888] The Ministry of Justice and Public Security and the Ministry of Defence are jointly responsible for ensuring that SBS and BFF are harmonised and correspond with measures across sectors

[1889] NBS is a framework that requires the preparation of underlying plans in order to have value as a decision-making tool

[1890] All ministries and subordinate agencies designated by the ministries must prepare their own emergency preparedness plans based on the NBS

[1891] The NBS is subject to regular audits, led by the Ministry of Justice and Public Security and the Ministry of Defense, to ensure that the measures are continuously quality assured and developed

[1892] The significant changes in the threat landscape mean that the government will conduct further impact assessments of the measures in the NBS to assess whether they are appropriate, feasible and realistic, and whether there are measures that are missing

[1893] The range of expertise in the area of total defence Society's vulnerability and preparedness challenges are continuously changing

[1894] This results in changed requirements for competence among central, regional and local emergency response actors

[1895] The Government sees a need to ensure that the expertise offered by total defence actors is updated, coordinated, relevant and of high quality

[1896] The government is concerned that there is good communication between different competence centres, so that the services and activities as a whole are utilized as efficiently as possible

[1897] Societal security in an uncertain world International law of war and the use of civilians

[1898] In armed conflict, Norway is obliged to follow the rules of the international law of war

[1899] In times of crisis and conflict, the Armed Forces will depend on services provided by civilian employees and civilian actors

[1900] Such support is permitted under the international law of war, but there are rules that limit how the support can be implemented

[1901] For example, the principle of distinction obliges the attacking party to protect civilian persons and objects from attack

[1902] Attacks should only be directed against lawful military targets

[1903] In addition, the principle of distinction obliges both the attacking and defending parties to protect civilians from the dangers of military operations

[1904] There are four consequences of the rules of international law of war that one must be aware of in order to safeguard the principle of distinction in civilian support for the Armed Forces

[1905] Civilians lose their protection against attacks under the principle of distinction as long as they participate directly in hostilities

[1906] The civilian becomes a legitimate target of attack

[1907] Civilians must therefore not be used in functions that involve direct participation in hostilities under the international law of war

[1908] Civilian objects may, under certain conditions, lose protection and become lawful targets, including if they are used for military purposes

[1909] c) It is permissible, within the framework of the principle of proportionality, under the international law of war to inflict civilian collateral damage when attacking military targets

[1910] Civilians who are on or near military targets are therefore at risk

[1911] The risk of collateral damage is a danger in military operations, from which civilians must be protected according to the principle of distinction

[1912] The risk of collateral damage must be managed through the focus on civilian support for the Armed Forces

[1913] d) Increasing civil-military cooperation may make it more difficult for an adversary to assess the distinction between civilians and military personnel, thereby weakening the protection of civilians according to the distinction principle

[1914] It is therefore important that civilians are not used in ways that deprive the opposing party of the ability to distinguish between objects that are lawful targets and combatants, and civilian objects and persons who must be protected from attack

[1915] Close civil-military cooperation therefore requires awareness of the rules for what are lawful objectives in the international law of war

[1916] The Ministry of Defence's subordinate agencies shall ensure that planning for and implementation of civilian support to the Armed Forces is in accordance with Norway's obligations under international law

[1917] The defense sector is required not to use civilians in functions that involve direct participation in hostilities

[1918] Such positions shall be filled by military personnel

[1919] When developing operational concepts, the defense sector must also consider whether there are limitations under the international law of war that must be taken into account, including limitations on the use of civilians

[1920] On the civilian side, it is essential that both public and private actors in the total defense have a dialogue with the Armed Forces about the organization of their civilian support, and adherence to the rules of the international law of war

[1921] A prerequisite for upholding the international law of war is competence, both in the private and public sectors

[1922] Competence development is therefore an important risk-reducing measure

[1923] Furthermore, contingency planning and scenario thinking are important tools for assessing the possible degree of cooperation in a security crisis or armed conflict

[1924] The international law of war should be included as an element in civil-military exercises

[1925] Societal security in an uncertain world Preventive national security

[1926] Norway is an open society that is built on a high degree of trust between citizens and between citizens and the state

[1927] A high level of trust facilitates innovation, value creation, good decision-making processes and cohesion

[1928] At the same time, several states or other actors continuously carry out intelligence activities and other security-threatening activities against Norway and Norwegian security interests

[1929] The activity may have the purpose, among other things, of gaining access to, or sabotaging, information or other values, or of undermining our democratic form of government

[1930] It is therefore important to build a security culture that maintains the high degree of trust and openness in Norwegian society, but that makes society aware of what may constitute security-threatening activities and how we can protect ourselves

[1931] The state has several instruments for protecting the values with the greatest importance for national security

[1932] As one of the most important instruments, the Storting has adopted a law on national security (the Security Act

[1933] The law entered into force on 1 January

[1934] This chapter emphasizes national security in the context of the Security Act

[1935] Implementation of the Security Act will contribute to a greater safeguarding of national security interests, including by requiring ministries to identify fundamental national functions (GNF) within their own areas of responsibility

[1936] GNFs are updated regularly and are stated in the annual budget proposals

[1937] National security has an interface with several topics in this report

[1938] Digital security is important in the work on national security, and the Security Act has its own provisions for safeguarding information and information systems, among other things

[1939] This report discusses digital security as a topic, both with the use of the Security Act and other instruments

[1942] Government policy

[1943] The Government will: – Ensure a holistic approach to the work of implementing the Security Act and identifying and securing objects and infrastructure worthy of protection

[1944] – Ensure that the National Security Authority (NSM) further develops expertise on how the risks associated with foreign investments can be prevented and countered

[1947] National security and the Security Act National security challenges must be solved with instruments that are adapted to an ever-changing threat and risk picture

[1948] The Security Act is a key instrument here

[1949] The concept of national security in the context of the Security Act is about safeguarding national security interests

[1950] In the law, national security interests are understood as the country's sovereignty, territorial integrity and democratic form of government, as well as overarching security policy interests related to: – the activities, security and freedom of action of the highest state bodies – defence, security and preparedness – relations with other states and international organisations Norway scores highly on international measurements of trust

[1951] See OECD, Government at a Glance

[1952] Core government results, the European Social Survey 2014 and the EU-SILC Survey of Living Conditions

[1953] Basic national functions

[1954] services, production and other forms of activity that are of such importance that a complete or partial loss of the function would have consequences for the state's ability to safeguard national security interests

[1955] Social security in an uncertain world – economic stability and freedom of action – the basic functionality of society and the basic security of the population

[1956] The scope of the Security Act is the area of state security and that part of the area of societal security that is of significant importance to the state's ability to safeguard national security interests

[1957] The Act is intended to help prevent, uncover and counteract security-threatening activities, that is, intentional actions that may directly or indirectly harm national security interests

[1958] The law is based on a risk-based approach and requires that businesses subject to the Security Act continuously assess the risk to which the business's assets are exposed, and that necessary measures are implemented to achieve adequate security

[1959] The law is also a tool for strengthening cooperation between authorities and businesses so that preventive safety work can be carried out in a more efficient and responsible manner, across all sectors of society

[1960] In addition, the law shall ensure that security measures are implemented in accordance with fundamental legal principles and values in a democratic society, and that necessary privacy interests are safeguarded

[1961] Identifying fundamental national functions (GNF) as part of the implementation of the Security Act lays the foundation for a more systematic follow-up of security over time (see box

[1962] GNF becomes the starting point for overall risk assessments and mapping of dependencies

[1963] Private enterprises that are of crucial importance to a GNF, or that process classified information, will be subject to the Security Act

[1964] GNF will also be a leader in identifying values ​​worthy of protection

[1965] If it proves necessary to identify GNF that does not naturally fall under the area of a particular ministry, the Ministry of Justice and Public Security will take responsibility for determining such GNF. There are a number of sector-specific regulations that regulate various security issues

[1966] The sector regulations exist together with the Safety Act and its underlying regulations

[1967] The sector regulations do not replace the requirements of the Security Act for businesses that are subject to the Security Act

[1968] However, compliance with sector regulations can contribute to meeting requirements in the Security Act

[2020] Organization of work on national security

[2021] The Safety Act states that preventive safety is a corporate responsibility

[2022] The law requires that the business implement the preventive security measures necessary to achieve a reasonable level of security and reduce the risk associated with security-threatening activities

[2023] As part of this work, the businesses must identify dependencies on other businesses, so that risk-reducing measures can be implemented where the dependency makes it necessary

[2024] Each minister is responsible for preventive security within his or her sector

[2025] This means following up on the fact that each business in the sector is working systematically on preventive safety work

[2026] In addition to the tasks that the Ministry of Justice and Public Security has as a sector ministry, the ministry also has overall responsibility for preventive security work on the civilian side, cf

[2027] The Ministry of Defence has similar responsibilities in the defence sector

[2028] NSM is the national professional and supervisory authority for preventive safety

[2029] NSM, as a security authority under the Security Act, shall, on behalf of the Ministry of Justice and Public Security and the Ministry of Defence, exercise overall cross-sectoral responsibility for national security in accordance with the Security Act

[2030] NSM is thus an agency that belongs to both the defense sector and the justice sector

[2031] A cross-sectoral security law and a national security authority with such cross-sectoral responsibility mean that we as a state are better equipped to safeguard our national security than some other states are

[2032] Some other states have a more fragmented regulatory framework without an authority with national professional and supervisory responsibility across the military and civilian sides, which makes comprehensive security work more demanding

[2033] It is important that we maintain and further develop this advantage

[2034] NSM shall, among other things, provide information, advice and guidance on preventive safety to businesses subject to the Safety Act

[2035] NSM also has important functions within operational tasks and incident management that are not limited to the Security Act, including, among other things, those related to the development of security measures and operational support to the Armed Forces

[2036] NSM shall coordinate the work between authorities that have a role in preventive digital security, and shall facilitate appropriate interaction between them

[2037] With effect from 3 May 2019, the administrative responsibility for the follow-up of NSM was transferred from the Ministry of Defence to the Ministry of Justice and Emergency Preparedness

[2038] From the same date, administrative responsibility for the Security Act was also transferred

[2039] The changes strengthen the work on national security on the civilian side, while maintaining a good link between the civilian side and the defense sector

[2040] The Government has thereby facilitated the Ministry of Justice and Public Security taking a clearer driving and coordinating role within national security on the civilian side

[2041] This role includes initiating and coordinating processes across ministries, guiding ministries in their work in the area, ensuring that issues across sectors are handled, and presenting matters of disagreement to the government, or if necessary, to the King in Council

[2042] In addition, it would be natural for the Ministry of Justice and Public Security, if necessary, by virtue of its coordination role, to identify general national functions in any areas that are not clearly covered by any ministry's area of responsibility

[2043] Royal Decree of 3 May on Changes in the ministerial structure and in the division of responsibilities between ministries

[2056] Priority areas of importance for national security

[2057] The following highlights areas that are considered to be of particular importance to national security in the coming years and that the government is working to address

[2058] Priority areas discussed in Chapter 8 will also be important for national security

[2059] Comprehensive implementation of the Security Act The Security Act is one of the most important and central instruments for safeguarding our national security (see section

[2060] In 2019 and 2020, significant work has been done across all sectors to identify fundamental national functions (GNF

[2061] Although much is in place, some work still remains, and the work must be seen as ongoing in the sense that the identified GNFs must be regularly reviewed to assess the need for adjustments as a result of societal developments

[2062] Objects worthy of protection that have been designated and secured under the old Security Act will maintain their classification until a renewed assessment of the need for continued designation and security has been made

[2063] A clear majority of the objects worthy of protection that were classified according to the previous regulations are objects where the function worthy of protection is dependent on ICT infrastructure and systems

[2064] Object security has previously been too largely equated with the physical security of material objects, which may contribute to security in the digital domain receiving too little attention

[2065] A threat actor with great capacity will be able to exploit various vulnerabilities to gain physical or digital access to an object or infrastructure, with subsequent negative consequences for national security interests

[2066] Protection must therefore be adapted and include both human, technological and organizational measures

[2067] The technological measures can be both digital and physical

[2068] The Security Act sets few specific requirements for how an information system, object or infrastructure worthy of protection should be secured

[2070] The risk assessment must take into account both the security-threatening activities that the information systems, objects and infrastructure may be exposed to and the probability of such activities

[2079] Unwanted investments in Norwegian businesses Threat and risk assessments from EOS services have highlighted that several states use economic instruments for purposes other than business

[2080] Investments and acquisitions can be used as a means to gain insight into sensitive information related to, for example, emergency preparedness arrangements, critical infrastructure and political decision-making processes

[2081] It can also provide access to technology and resources of strategic importance

[2082] Companies that develop high technology for use in industries of strategic importance are particularly vulnerable

[2083] The purchase of strategically located properties may, for example, be intended to provide a platform for covert intelligence activities against Norwegian and allied military activity

[2084] Unwanted investments in Norwegian businesses can result in states with which Norway does not have security policy cooperation being placed in a position where they gain influence that conflicts with our national security interests

[2085] The use of promises of investments or threats to withdraw them can also be used as a means of pressure on other states

[2086] See also Chapter 9 on composite threats

[2087] Each individual investment, acquisition or financing of, for example, research and development projects will often be unproblematic in isolation

[2088] Taken as a whole, and in light of the fact that some states work very long-term with instruments that apparently appear to be purely commercial interests, these investments may be incompatible with national security interests

[2089] Addressing these challenges therefore involves, among other things, looking at a country's economic engagement in Norway overall and over time

[2090] The threat and risk picture that some foreign investments can represent is common to many European and Western countries

[2091] The knowledge that some states use investments and acquisitions as strategic instruments is causing several European countries, as well as the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, to consider measures to reduce the risk associated with foreign investments

[2092] Some countries have developed and use screening mechanisms to identify and manage this risk

[2093] The EU has adopted a regulation on foreign direct investment, which entered into force in 2019. The regulation facilitates information exchange and coordination between EU Member States, and between Member States and the Commission, on the screening of and possible prohibitions on acquisitions from third countries

[2094] It is up to each individual member state whether a national screening mechanism should be established or continued

[2095] The member states decide how the mechanisms should be designed, but the regulation sets certain minimum requirements for what the national screening mechanisms must contain

[2096] The regulation also expresses the importance of international cooperation in countering unwanted foreign investments

[2097] It is very relevant for Norway to seek to cooperate with the EU in this area, both in order to be able to receive relevant information in the processing of such investment cases nationally, but also out of consideration for Norwegian businesses that export to the EU so that the EU regime does not unintentionally have negative consequences for them

[2098] The EU's interpretation of the terms "screening" and "direct investment" is set out in the EU's Foreign Investment Screening Regulation, which entered into force in April

[2099] The EU defines screening as follows

[2100] Screening means a procedure allowing to assess, investigate, authorize, condition, prohibit or unwind foreign direct investments

[2101] The term encompasses both the process related to information input and retrieval (detection), and the decision-making process related to assessment and handling (action

[2102] The EU uses the term "direct investment" to refer to investments that can provide the opportunity to gain influence in a company and that go beyond mergers and acquisitions

[2103] For example, establishing debt dependencies could be a key tool for exerting pressure on a business

[2104] The EU definition also includes investments in the value chain of the business that holds the value

[2105] The purpose of including this type of investment in the definition is to prevent threat actors from circumventing the regulations and securing entry into the value chain that is not screened, in order to then gain influence over A screening mechanism is a tool for capturing and assessing the intention behind an investment, as well as who is actually behind it. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT

[2106] St. 5 Social security in an uncertain world the value

[2107] Mapping value chains is therefore central to this work

[2108] It is appropriate that Norway, in our work, uses the same conceptual understanding of "screening" and "direct investment" as the EU

[2109] This will, among other things, facilitate the work of building a common platform for cooperation and expertise across national borders, and we will therefore take the EU's use of terminology as a starting point in further work on this issue

[2112] This means that a decision can also have retroactive effect

[2122] Implementation of new technology as an opportunity and challenge

[2123] Digitalization provides major benefits and contributes to both value creation, welfare and, in several ways, improved social security in a normal situation

[2124] However, the extensive digitalization and increasing dependence on digital solutions for all key societal functions leads to new vulnerabilities in devices and networks

[2125] This can be exploited by threat actors to acquire information and/or values by establishing backdoors into digital systems, exploiting enormous volumes of data generated and processed through digital solutions, or sabotaging the critical dependence of certain societal functions on technological and digital solutions

[2126] See also the discussion of digital security in Chapter

[2127] A challenge going forward will be the extensive interconnection of systems that are currently considered relatively independent and autonomous

[2128] One dimension is the amount of data that can be viewed in context, but an equally big challenge is the sharp increase in signals required for wireless communication

[2129] Certain state actors want to exploit vulnerabilities in such systems and in themselves pose a significant risk if this is used to affect societal functions

[2130] In addition, the increased commercial use of wireless communication in the various dimensions (land, air, space) will pose a significant risk of unintentional interference with signals on which societal functions depend

[2131] The increase in the importance and spread of wireless communication and different regulations in different countries mean that unintentional interference can occur and sometimes have major societal consequences

[2159] The human factor Foreign intelligence services spend large resources recruiting both Norwegian citizens and their own citizens who live in Norway and who have access to information or other assets that are of importance to the state in question

[2160] An insider is a current or former employee, consultant or contractor who has or has had legitimate access to the company's systems, procedures, objects and information, and who misuses this knowledge and access to carry out actions that cause damage or loss to the company

[2161] Personnel safety is a prerequisite for businesses to be able to achieve a reasonable level of safety

[2162] Personnel security is about preventing, detecting and counteracting security-threatening activities committed by people who have legitimate access to the assets we want to protect

[2163] This work includes, among other things, managing human vulnerabilities and ensuring that the human factor in security work contributes to strengthening security and not weakening it

[2164] To gain access to information classified CONFIDENTIAL or higher, the person must be security cleared, but anyone with access to classified or sensitive information is a potential target for foreign intelligence

[2165] Insider risk has been highlighted by, among others, PST and NSM as a significant risk, with very high potential for damage, to national security interests

[2166] Externally directed, and often very expensive, security measures lose their effectiveness if there is an insider with access through their employment who can knowingly or unknowingly provide the threat actor with information or access

[2167] NSM has drawn up basic principles for personnel safety, see box

[2171] Quality improvement for the clearance process

[2172] The Civilian Clearance Authority was established as a directorate under the Ministry of Justice and Public Security with responsibility for being the central clearance authority on the civilian side

[2173] Experience so far clearly shows that this is a quality boost for the clearance process

[2174] There are now two central clearance authorities in Norway for the military and civilian side respectively

[2175] These have extensive interaction

[2176] There are still some minor clearance authorities in certain specific areas such as for the legislative branch, the judiciary, the EOS services and the Prime Minister's Office

[2177] In the long term, there may be grounds for considering further consolidation of the clearance authorities

[2178] NSM has also been strengthened as a professional authority within personnel safety

[2179] The current process of security and access clearance under the Security Act is highly manual and largely characterized by paper-based solutions

[2180] This is both resource- and time-consuming

[2181] In order to develop and implement a modern digital solution, NSM's basic principles for personnel security define a set of principles that address the human aspect of preventing, detecting and handling insider trading and other undesirable actions

[2182] The basic principles of personnel safety aim to assist businesses in finding the right personnel safety measures

[2183] The main focus of the fundamental principles is what businesses can do to prevent, detect and handle insider trading, i.e. cases where current or former employees cause or have caused damage or loss to the business through misuse of their knowledge and/or access

[2184] The basic principles also recommend measures that also help prevent or counteract other forms of undesirable actions

[2185] These measures can help increase the company's resilience to securitythreatening activities by enabling employees to reduce risk in the event of incidents

[2186] The basic principles are cross-sectoral and provide recommendations for all businesses that wish to safeguard personnel safety

[2187] For the clearance process, as well as to automate case processing where possible, NOK 20 million has been allocated

[2188] The government aims to continue the increased allocation in the period

[2189] The measures involve both increased efficiency and better resource utilization, while also contributing to an increased degree of legal certainty and equal treatment

[2190] Personnel safety across the entire crisis spectrum

[2191] Personnel safety is crucial to our ability to handle emergency and crisis situations

[2192] It is absolutely crucial that personnel in the total defense are security-capable to safeguard our national security interests

[2193] It is through the security clearance process that we build this preparedness

[2194] A crisis situation could result in demands for increased deliveries from the clearance authorities

[2195] It is therefore crucial that we are able to exercise personnel security both at the local and national levels, throughout the entire crisis spectrum, and that the clearance authorities have the necessary tools for this

[2196] Furthermore, it is important to see personnel safety as one of several preventive safety measures under the Safety Act, which are intended to help reduce the risk to which a business is exposed in a normal situation

[2197] The Ministry of Justice and Public Security and the Ministry of Defence will therefore investigate whether the organisation, structure and instruments of the NSM, the Defence Security Department and the Civilian Clearance Authority are adapted to the implementation of personnel security throughout the entire crisis spectrum

[2198] Need for research-based knowledge about personnel security vulnerabilities

[2199] Targeted countermeasures against insider risk are a complex task that requires significant expertise and focus on more than just the clearance, as human vulnerabilities can arise or change during the period of time the person is cleared

[2200] The work of preventing and countering insider trading can be demanding

[2201] A driving factor for this is that Norwegian society is increasingly internationalized

[2202] More and more people are pursuing education and work in other countries, and Norway is dependent on a corresponding flow of expertise and human resources to Norway

[2203] This also means that family structures and contact networks are becoming increasingly globalized

[2204] Technology, the internet and social media are key factors of change in a more globalized society, also within personnel safety

[2205] Good personnel security also includes a focus on the fact that human vulnerabilities can arise in the digital space

[2206] Traditional loyalty to the state is changing as parallel, and in some cases competing, loyalties to other states, individuals or groups are developing

[2207] Globalization also presents challenges related to secure identity and the ability to check the background of people who will have access to our values

[2208] Connections to other countries, people or groups can make a person vulnerable

[2209] Other countries' intelligence services will exploit such vulnerabilities, and it is therefore important that we have good systems for handling this throughout the entire period a person has access to information, objects or infrastructure

[2210] The Government will therefore ensure that we increase our research-based knowledge about countering insider risk

[2487] The committee believes that digital security must be better safeguarded in the Government's standard procurement agreements, and that guidance on digital security in procurement must be further developed

[2647] Societal security in an uncertain world Composite threats

[2648] Threats are situations where an actor uses a range of means to influence us

[2649] Disinformation, investments in business, corruption, harassment of government officials, influencing elections, recruiting or placing unfaithful servants in commercial or public enterprises, and digital attacks are examples of possible means of action

[2650] The agents can be used separately or combined and coordinated so that they support and reinforce each other

[2651] They can also be used over a long period of time

[2652] Norwegian citizens, politicians, and public and private enterprises may be exposed to such use of instruments

[2653] The combined use of instruments may aim to destabilize society in order to make it more vulnerable

[2654] In a possible situation where we find ourselves close to or in a military conflict, the use of military means can be combined with non-military means to achieve the greatest possible effect (see also box

[2655] The potential breadth of the use of instruments makes it challenging to establish the best possible understanding of the situation across sectors and different instruments

[2656] The work against complex threats is closely related to the work on preventive national security (see Chapter

[2657] When actors seek to influence important institutions such as elections, or undermine trust in authorities and democratic institutions, it could affect our national security interests

[2658] The work must also be seen in connection with the work to further develop total defence (see Chapter 6) and the work on digital security (see Chapter 8). Purpose

[2659] The use of composite instruments can have different purposes

[2660] It may include attempts to influence the implementation of specific time-bound activities or situations, such as a political election

[2661] Furthermore, the purpose may be to complicate decision-making processes or influence decisions so that the outcome suits the interests of the actor behind the use of the instrument to the greatest extent possible

[2662] Another and more long-term goal may be to weaken the existing social order and the foundation on which liberal democracies are built

[2663] This can be done by weakening trust between citizens, businesses and governments, and by undermining confidence in public institutions and public authorities and their ability to carry out their tasks

[2664] This can create better conditions for those behind the use of instruments to influence the public debate and in other ways

[2665] There is no uniform definition of the concepts of composite threats and hybrid threats

[2666] The terms are often used interchangeably and synonymously to describe situations where an actor uses different instruments in combination to influence us

[2667] Individually, the various instruments can pose a threat, for example to critical infrastructure, to information we want to protect, or to the pillars of our democracy

[2668] Such pillars can be trust in authorities, trust between people and between groups of people, and a free democratic debate

[2669] When several instruments are used together, they can support each other and increase the overall effect

[2670] For example, a digital attack against critical infrastructure, such as a computer network, could be attempted combined with a disinformation campaign that Norwegian authorities lack the ability to ensure Norwegian citizens have safe access to the internet

[2671] Then the threats to our society are complex and affect across sectors

[2672] In this White Paper, the term composite threats (and not hybrid threats) is used precisely to emphasize that both threats and the use of instruments can be composed of different components

[2673] St. 5 Social security in an uncertain world attempt to influence societal development in a direction that can serve their interests

[2674] Political issues can be made subject to external influence, not necessarily by providing support for a particular political position, but by fueling polarization in society

[2675] The use of instruments aimed at more time-limited activities, such as a political election, can also have a long-term effect

[2676] If, for example, an actor manages to create doubt about whether an election has been conducted without undue influence, it can weaken people's trust in the authorities' ability to conduct free elections

[2677] This, in turn, may contribute to weakening general trust in the authorities

[2678] Combined use of instruments can be used across the entire crisis spectrum, i.e. both in peacetime, in security crises and as part of military conflicts

[2679] In the upper part of the crisis spectrum, both the scope and the degree of coordination of the use of instruments are expected to increase

[2680] It can help tie up resources, increase the degree of confusion, and reduce the ability to deal with the military threat

[2681] It can also increase the overall effect of the use of the policy

[2682] The use of military instruments will logically become more prominent higher up the crisis spectrum

[2683] At the lower end of the crisis spectrum, there is a greater possibility that the use of instruments is less coordinated, but such use of instruments can still cause harm

[2684] An example could be a digital attack against a sector, where the actor behind the attack tests the ability to penetrate the system

[2685] Such an attack can be challenging to handle, and reduce the usability of the system while the attack is ongoing

[2686] In addition, information collected at the lower end of the crisis spectrum could also be used in a situation higher up the crisis spectrum

[2699] Challenges in the effort to combat complex threats The effort to combat complex threats has four main elements

[2700] detection (discovering incidents), identification (understanding the purpose of the use of the means), attribution (discovering who is behind it) and reaction (handling the incident

[2701] Both detection and identification can be demanding because the actors behind them will often seek to arrange the instruments in such a way that it is difficult to reveal whether they are actually an attempt to influence

[2702] For example, a foreign investment in Norwegian business (see section 7.5.2 and below) may be a legitimate and desired action, but it may also be a covert attempt at influence

[2703] It can also be challenging to uncover whether an observed single incident is part of a more complex use of instruments

[2704] Individual events can occur in different sectors, within private and public activities, and at different times in relation to each other

[2705] It can therefore be challenging to see individual events in context and to form a holistic understanding of the situation

[2706] Attribution (revealing which actors are behind the use of policy instruments) also raises challenges

[2707] This is especially true in the digital space, where there are good opportunities to hide where an attack comes from

[2708] In addition, actors behind the use of instruments will often act covertly

[2709] Non-state actors can act on behalf of state actors, making it difficult to determine who is actually behind the use of instruments

[2710] Actors behind the use of instruments will attempt to exploit existing vulnerabilities

[2711] Such vulnerabilities may be the result of deliberate policy

[2712] An example is investments from foreign players in Norwegian businesses

[2713] Such investments are an important tool

[2714] in open and market- Report

[2715] St. 5 2020–2021 Social security in an uncertain world based economies like the Norwegian one

[2716] They can provide Norwegian companies with access to capital and expertise

[2717] Investments and acquisitions can also pose a security risk in that the actors behind the investments can gain access to sensitive information and technology (see also section

[2718] Another example is how disagreements that are part of normal political discourse can be exploited, for example through disinformation or the use of straw men to create discord between different groups in the population

[2719] State and non-state actors who seek to influence others for their own benefit will use the means they have available at any given time and find appropriate

[2720] However, developments within the digital space provide completely new opportunities, including the ability to adapt, disseminate and change information, and to move instruments from one sector to another

[2721] It is also a challenge that a great deal of infrastructure is connected to the internet, and can therefore be influenced and sabotaged using digital means

[2722] In addition, in recent years, there has been a clear willingness to use such instruments

[2723] Russia's use of instruments in Ukraine and the attempt to influence the 2017 US election are two examples

[2724] Incidents that are suspected of falling under the category of composite threats must be followed up appropriately

[2725] Foreign states' intelligence and influence attempts against Norway and Norwegian interests, or suspected attempts at such influence, are handled on a daily basis by the Police Security Service (PST), the Intelligence Service (E-service) and the National Security Authority (NSM

[2726] This is regulated through the Police Act, the Intelligence Services Act and the Security Act with associated regulations

[2727] The Government's work against complex threats

[2728] The work against composite

[2729] Threats affect all ministries and a number of underlying businesses

[2730] A good understanding of the threat landscape and of one's own vulnerabilities across sectors is crucial for this work

[2731] Based on such knowledge, vulnerabilities can be reduced, undesirable incidents can be prevented, and handling capabilities can be strengthened

[2732] The preparation and maintenance of systematic risk and vulnerability analyses is therefore an important element in the work against complex threats

[2733] The requirement in the Public Safety Instructions that all ministries must prepare and maintain such analyses is therefore important, as are the requirements that ministries with primary responsibility for critical societal functions must ensure that such analyses are prepared for the functions for which the ministry is responsible

[2734] Similar provisions are provided in laws and other regulations within various sectors

[2735] Good coordination between different sector authorities is very important in order to see the overall threat picture

[2736] In addition, a large proportion of critical infrastructure is owned and operated by private actors, and a number of Norwegian private and semi-governmental enterprises develop knowledge and technology that may be of interest to foreign actors

[2737] It is therefore also important to have good dialogue between the authorities and private and semi-governmental agencies about the threat landscape and about any incidents that may be part of the complex use of instruments

[2738] Furthermore, it is important that Norwegian businesses report incidents they suspect may be an attempt at influence

[2739] Businesses that are subject to the Security Act are obliged to report security-threatening activities or suspicions of such activities to the security authority (NSM

[2740] Knowledge from Norwegian businesses about the threat landscape could be of great importance for central authorities to obtain the most comprehensive possible situational picture and the best possible basis for handling threats

[2741] Although vulnerability-reducing measures are important, it is neither desirable nor possible to establish a society that fully prevents vulnerabilities from arising

[2742] We cannot therefore prevent foreign actors from finding vulnerabilities to exploit in the future

[2743] Awareness that vulnerabilities can be exploited is in itself a prerequisite for us to be able to prevent this from happening to the greatest extent possible

[2744] This awareness must be found in both public administration, private businesses and individual citizens

[2745] The following are key elements in the government's work against complex threats

[2746] Several of the points are of a more permanent nature and therefore ongoing work

[2747] The measures supplement other work the government is doing related to intelligence threats against Norway, and the authorities' measures against the most serious threats to the country's security

[2748] The measures must also be seen in the context of the points under Responsibilities and coordination mechanisms in the ministries have been clarified

[2749] The Ministry of Justice and Public Security is assigned the main responsibility for coordinating the government's work

[2750] Significant parts of the more specific measures the government has implemented are graded according to the Security Act

[2751] They cannot therefore be discussed in detail

[2752] St. 5 Societal security in an uncertain world linked to complex threats directed against civilians

[2753] The work is carried out in close dialogue with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defence and other relevant ministries

[2754] – The expertise and dialogue between ministries on the combined use of policy instruments is strengthened

[2755] All ministries have designated contact points for work on complex threats. – The government is further developing the work on compiling information on various incidents that may be part of a complex use of instruments, in order to obtain the best possible situational understanding

[2756] In this work, the Police Security Service, the Intelligence Service and the National Security Authority play important roles

[2757] The Norwegian Police Directorate, the Directorate for Public Security and Emergency Preparedness and other relevant directorates and agencies are involved when necessary

[2758] – Dialogue with private and semi-state actors has been strengthened. – Work against disinformation has been strengthened, see point 9.6 below

[2761] Disinformation can form a significant part of a complex use of instruments, but it can also be a potent instrument in itself

[2762] In light of the sharp increase in the use of social media and changes in people's media use, as well as the increased opportunities that digitalization provides to communicate and influence through various digital platforms, the work against disinformation is a central part of the work against complex threats

[2763] Disinformation involves deliberately misleading information and arguments to influence public debate or decision-making, or to undermine democratic processes

[2764] More generally, disinformation can have two main purposes: – To divert attention from a topic, polarize social debates, cover up the truth or attempt to influence actors to act in a certain way

[2765] An example is attempts to influence elections, as several countries have experienced in recent years. – Attempting to influence the “knowledge space” where authorities, businesses, groups and individuals develop knowledge, form their opinions and make decisions

[2766] These may be more long-term processes where the goal is, for example, to destabilize the foundation on which liberal democracies are built (for example, weakening trust between groups, trust in the media, in democratic institutions such as elections, etc

[2767] Disinformation can be carried out using a number of different means

[2768] Text, images, video and audio can be manipulated to distort the message

[2769] Information can be fabricated and presented as true

[2770] Fake experts can be used to undermine debates or turn them in a desired direction

[2771] The other party can be inundated with a flood of arguments and facts that make it more challenging to sort out what is important and correct

[2772] Demonstrations can be organized to give a false impression of support for a cause

[2773] One can attempt to attack and discredit people who hold a particular view

[2774] In addition, these and other instruments can be combined in different ways, and disinformation can take place on different platforms such as printed media (newspapers, magazines and books), social media, television and radio

[2775] Actors in Norway can also use disinformation to achieve their goals

[2776] These may be individuals or representatives of special interests

[2777] However, it is important to emphasize that freedom of expression remains a matter of course

[2778] However, the work against disinformation must have a broader perspective than activities from state actors or those who may operate on their behalf

[2779] Disinformation has been a significant challenge for many countries during the coronavirus pandemic

[2780] Such information can weaken society's support for and the effect of the authorities' measures, and be a threat to public health

[2781] For example, as of July 2020, the EU had uncovered 3.4 million Twitter accounts with what was considered questionable information about COVID

[2782] NATO also reports that alliance members and allies have experienced the spread of disinformation during the pandemic

[2783] In Norway, the challenges have been limited, but given that the pandemic could last a long time, it is important to maintain focus on this threat

[2784] Work against disinformation Preparedness against and handling disinformation raises various challenges

[2785] These affect authorities in all sectors, but also private businesses, organizations and individual citizens

[2786] Social security in an uncertain world

[2787] – The ability to critique sources

[2788] A prerequisite for counteracting disinformation is being able to assess the sender and the credibility of the news and knowledge sources used

[2789] Developing the ability to critique sources begins in school, but it must also be developed and maintained in organizations, private businesses, public agencies, and individual citizens

[2790] – The ability to analyze information flows

[2791] The best possible understanding of attempts at influence through disinformation requires that authorities and others can identify attempts at influence on different media platforms and see these in context. – The role of the media

[2792] A good, diverse, independent, critical and self-critical press that the population trusts is a central part of protection against fake news and disinformation

[2793] The press's role as infrastructure in the public discourse can only be fulfilled if the media are – and not least are perceived to be – independent of the power structures they are supposed to monitor, primarily public authorities

[2794] This places limitations on what the authorities can and should do, and on which instruments are suitable for, among other things, combating disinformation and fake news

[2795] Understanding and possibly countering disinformation requires the ability to understand who is behind it

[2796] Attribution involves identifying and possibly holding an actor responsible for an intentional action

[2797] Attribution can also be a tool in itself, because authorities may want to show that they know who is behind disinformation and other attempts at influence

[2798] Whether it is desirable and appropriate to hold an actor responsible for an intended action may depend on the information base and the political context. – Technological competence

[2799] A significant part of disinformation occurs in the digital space

[2800] Awareness of how technology is used for disinformation and other influence is crucial (see also Chapter 8 on digital security

[2801] This includes knowledge about how fake news / disinformation is spread online, how social media can be misused and how such influence can be automated

[2802] Influencing elections Covert influencing of elections is a threat to liberal democracies

[2803] There was increased attention to the security of the election process in the parliamentary elections

[2804] Attention was particularly focused on the technical solutions used in the machine counting of ballots

[2805] To avoid any doubt as to whether the election results were correct, and to ensure that confidence in the election was not undermined, the Ministry of Local Government and Modernisation issued a regulation 10 days before election day requiring municipalities to count all ballots manually in the preliminary count

[2806] In February 2019, a similar provision was adopted in the election regulations, which applied from the municipal, board and county council elections onwards

[2807] Undesirable events such as communication breakdowns and errors in the electronic election administration (EVA) system are the most likely risks in the conduct of elections

[2808] Influence on political processes and digital attacks against EVA are considered the most relevant external threats

[2809] In addition, hacking to demonstrate weaknesses or cast doubt on the integrity of the system is believed to be a threat

[2810] During the 2018 Swedish parliamentary elections, several attempts to influence the political processes were uncovered

[2840] Ability to critique sources

[2841] In an increasingly fragmented media landscape, and where several media outlets are not subject to the same editorial control as more traditional media outlets, the ability to critique sources is a very important component in the work of preventing the effects of disinformation and other attempts at influence

[2842] School plays an important role in developing the ability to critique sources

[2843] Critical thinking, source criticism and source use have been reinforced in the new curriculum, which will be implemented in schools from the autumn

[2844] Based on Report

[2845] St. 28 (2015–

[2846] the government has renewed the curricula for all subjects in primary and lower secondary education and the core subjects in upper secondary education

[2847] The curricula will become more relevant, students will have more time for in-depth learning, and there will be better coherence between the different parts of the curriculum

[2848] The five basic skills of reading, writing, arithmetic, digital and oral skills are made clear in the subjects

[2849] Digital skills have gained a clearer place in the new curricula

[2850] This includes important aspects of digital citizenship such as good digital judgment, source criticism and information and data security, but also digital creativity, programming and algorithmic thinking

[2851] The definition of competence in professional renewal

[2852] emphasizes that critical thinking and reflection are an important part of what students should learn

[2853] Competence is being able to acquire and apply knowledge and skills to master challenges and solve tasks in familiar and unfamiliar contexts and situations

[2854] Competence involves understanding and the ability to reflect and think critically

[2855] Source criticism and source use are included in curricula for several subjects, and the topics are included as part of the basic skills in reading, mathematics, and digital skills

[2856] Source criticism and source use are also linked to the interdisciplinary theme of democracy and citizenship, which is included in most subjects

[2857] The interdisciplinary theme should provide students with knowledge about the prerequisites, values ​​and rules of democracy, and enable them to participate in democratic processes

[2858] Students will practice the ability to think critically, learn to handle differences of opinion and respect disagreement

[2859] Through work on the topic, students will learn why democracy cannot be taken for granted, and that it must be developed and maintained

[2860] Box 9.3 shows examples of competence objectives from various subjects where source criticism and source use are central

[2861] The government will introduce the new curriculum in stages from the start of school in the autumn

[2869] It shows that the editorially controlled press has a special role and function in democracy as a "public watchdog

[2870] This task presupposes that the press is independent of the power structures it is supposed to monitor, and that the public has confidence in this independence

[2871] Only then will content disseminated in the media provide a basis for free and informed political opinion formation

[2872] Editorial independence is therefore an absolute prerequisite for the function of editorially controlled journalistic media in the public discourse

[2873] The authorities must therefore be cautious about measures that could be perceived as attempts to influence editorial decisions or practices

[2874] The main purpose of policy in this area is therefore to facilitate a diversity of independent media

[2875] They should be able to function as open and independent channels for information exchange and public debate, managed according to agreed principles of press ethics

[2876] This is done both through economic framework conditions (for example, VAT exemption, direct media support and the financing of NRK) and through legal framework conditions (for example, legal regulations on editorial independence, editor's responsibility and source protection

[2880] Challenges related to social media and other platforms

[2881] Digitalization has fundamentally changed the conditions for freedom of expression, both in terms of production, dissemination and consumption of content and services

[2882] The emergence of electronic platforms and social media has led to an explosive expansion of individuals' access to information and opportunities for expression

[2883] At the same time, the traditional Article 10 of the ECHR states that everyone has the right to freedom of expression, which includes freedom to hold opinions and to receive and impart information and ideas without interference by public authority and regardless of frontiers

[2885] Preventive measures related to source criticism in the media area: Educational programs about source criticism and fake news

[2886] The Norwegian Media Authority, in collaboration with the Directorate of Education and Faktisk.no, has developed a teaching program to strengthen young people's critical understanding of the media

[2887] The program is intended for young people between the ages of 13 and 16 (junior high school

[2889] and the Norwegian Media Authority's Children and Media 2018 shows that young people between the ages of 9 and 18 have social media as their most important source of news

[2890] It is therefore important to strengthen young people's critical media understanding and vulnerability to believing and sharing fake news that is widespread on social media

[2891] The teaching plan can be used by teachers in schools or, for example, as part of confirmation education and is designed so that it can meet several competence goals in social studies and Norwegian for the age group

[2892] Issues that young people work on through this program include how to distinguish facts from opinions, what characterizes fake news, and why some people make up such stories

[2893] The teaching program was downloaded nearly 3,500 times

[2895] The Norwegian Media Authority's survey on critical media understanding shows that six out of ten people over 60 have low digital media understanding and over half of those over 60 did not recognize a single piece of fake news in the survey

[2896] Older people also have fewer methods for finding out whether a matter is true or false

[2898] Many people over 60 have lower digital skills than other age groups, and this may have an impact on their critical understanding of the media

[2900] St. 5 2020–2021 Social security in an uncertain world The editors' function as gatekeepers and filters against the negative aspects of freedom of expression – such as hatred, incitement, bullying and disinformation – has been weakened in the new media landscape

[2901] Large global media platforms for uploading and sharing content have taken on a new gatekeeper role, with significant influence on the digital discourse

[2902] It is debatable whether the platforms have in certain cases acquired such a dominant position that their terms of use, algorithms and moderation in practice function as a general framework for freedom of expression

[2903] An open internet is vulnerable to abuse

[2904] When anyone can publish content immediately, without editorial control based on industry ethical standards and guidelines, it will also affect the quality of what is published

[2905] The structure of the Internet and the rise of social media have made it easier than before to spread propaganda and disinformation to advance political or commercial interests

[2906] This may involve manipulation of the public, and lead to weakened trust in the public

[2907] Unfounded claims of “fake news” can be used as a means to weaken trust in critical media

[2908] Algorithms and artificial intelligence have become an integral part of the information society, and are used, among other things, to select, prioritize and target content to individual users, as well as to remove content that violates user terms

[2909] The use of such instruments places great demands on both private actors and the authorities, who must ensure that their use does not conflict with freedom of expression and other fundamental rights

[2920] Box 9.5 Examples of the media's work against disinformation

[2921] Faktisk.no is an initiative against fake news and disinformation in the public sphere, established and run by the media themselves

[2923] The organization also has as part of its mandate to “uncover and prevent the spread of fabricated messages that pose as real news.”

[2924] Faktisk.no was created by VG, Dagbladet, NRK and TV

[2926] As of October 2020, Faktisk.no has published 397 fact checks and 206 articles

[2927] The service checks exclusively factual claims and the selection of claims that are checked follows traditional news criteria such as materiality, proximity, topicality and sensation

[2934] Social Security in an Uncertain World to the Media Support Act establishes a new model for media support that will contribute to predictable financial frameworks for the media and strengthen the media's independence

[2935] A new media responsibility law (Act on Editorial Independence and Responsibility in Editor-Controlled Journalistic Media) came into force on 1 July

[2936] The law is intended to create incentives for serious management and control of the media based on journalistic norms and principles

[2937] This is done, among other things, by imposing stricter responsibility on the editor for the editorial content than would otherwise result from general legal rules

[2938] The law also means that the editor is given certain duties that will help build upon the rules of press ethics

[2939] Among other things, the editor is obliged to keep user-generated content separate from editorial content, to provide information about content that has not been pre-edited, and to provide information about the rules that apply to use of the forum

[2951] The initiative for concrete measures against disinformation in the media should come from and be led by the media themselves

[2952] This is crucial for the public's trust in the media's independence and ability to conduct critical journalism, facilitate political debate, and monitor political processes and decisions

[2953] It is also important that the authorities have a good dialogue with the media industry on these issues and provide assistance when needed

[2954] Strategic communication Strategic communication can be described as a state or non-state actor's planned and coordinated use of all communicative means to promote its own interests and achieve its objectives

[2955] The main purpose is to influence the target group's perceptions and/or behavior

[2956] Communication can take place through both words and actions, traditional and social media, diplomacy, bilateral talks and through other channels

[2957] The communication may concern current events, the threat landscape, official policy and/or measures taken by the authorities

[2958] Strategic communication can include attempts to influence us from a foreign actor, and can also be a tool in the implementation of military operations

[2959] The importance of strategic communication must be seen in light of the increasing potential for disinformation

[2960] As the number of platforms that can be used for disinformation increases, and we simultaneously see an increasing willingness among certain actors to try and influence through the information domain, it becomes even more important for Norwegian authorities to be able to communicate quickly and precisely what they think about a given threat or incident

[2961] Such communication can be an important part of preventive work, by trying to reduce the effect of the influence of foreign actors

[2962] The Norwegian authorities' strategic communication aimed at their own population must always be truthful

[2963] The Government is continuously developing its expertise and work to handle strategic communication

[2964] Strategic communication is also discussed in more detail in the Ministry of Defence's long-term plan for the defence sector

[2969] Social security in an uncertain world 9.8 International work

[2970] Composite threats are high on the agenda in NATO, the EU, and other international forums

[2971] The challenges faced by different countries, for example, with regard to establishing situational awareness, countering disinformation or preventing election influence, are largely similar

[2972] International exchange of experiences about the threat landscape, possible measures and experiences from handling specific threats is therefore of great value

[2973] At the same time, several countries may be exposed to similar and even simultaneous attempts at influence

[2974] Good international cooperation is therefore of great importance in order to be able to quickly notify each other and, if necessary, coordinate measures and reactions

[2975] International cooperation is therefore an important element in the government's work against complex threats

[2976] In 2017, Norway joined the “Center of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats” in Helsinki, Finland

[2977] The center was established in 2017 at the request of the EU and with support from NATO

[2978] It is open to countries that are members of NATO and/or the EU

[2979] As of 1 October 2020, 27 countries are members

[2980] Canada, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Greece, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Montenegro, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Spain, United Kingdom, Sweden, Czech Republic, Turkey, Germany, Hungary, USA and Austria

[2981] NATO and the EU are also participating

[2982] There is a high level of activity at the center, primarily through a number of different professional meetings on relevant issues

[2983] The center has three permanent working groups

[2984] Influence

[2985] Resilience and

[2986] Strategy and defense

[2987] Norway, through the Ministry of Defense, is the lead nation in NATO for the alliance's integrity program

[2988] This aims to strengthen integrity in member countries, partners and the NATO organization, as well as reduce the risk of corruption and other undesirable influence

[2989] Composite threats are also a topic in the Nordic societal security work, the so-called Haga cooperation

[2990] This collaboration was politically initiated

[2991] The common overall goal is to strengthen the Nordic countries' ability to prevent and reduce the consequences of major accidents, natural and man-made disasters, and other societal crises within the emergency preparedness area

[2992] The new and changing threat landscape has shown that work on societal security cannot be viewed from a limited, national perspective, but requires cross-border cooperation

[2993] The ability to provide mutual assistance across borders in the event of serious incidents is of great importance

[2994] Norway also participates in other international forums where topics related to complex threats are discussed, including issues related to disinformation, strategic communication, foreign state investments and electoral influence

[2995] Societal security in an uncertain world Prevention and preparedness locally and regionally

[2996] All events that occur occur in a municipality

[2997] Extreme weather and floods, major accidents, fires and epidemics are examples of the wide range of unwanted events that can affect counties and municipalities

[2998] At the same time, important societal functions and services are being digitalized

[2999] This makes the risk picture more complex and changeable

[3000] The events and developments in the risk picture are putting preparedness at the local and regional level to the test

[3001] Municipal and regional levels have key roles in the work on societal security, and also an independent responsibility for ensuring digital security

[3002] In this work, it is crucial that local and regional authorities have the tools and authorities they need to be able to conduct good spatial planning and implement necessary measures

[3003] Community safety actors at local and regional levels must have expertise in the challenges and be well coordinated

[3004] There is reason to expect that as a result of climate change, we will experience more and more serious natural events in the years to come

[3005] Both the individual sector and the individual level of administration have an independent responsibility for reducing the consequences of climate change within their own area of responsibility

[3006] At the same time, climate adaptation is an issue that affects societal security across all sectors

[3007] This requires good arenas for collaboration on challenges and solutions between societal security actors

[3008] Municipalities and county governors' offices must facilitate such coordination and be drivers for ensuring comprehensive and systematic social security work regionally and locally

[3009] This chapter focuses on the responsibilities and roles of municipalities and county governors, as well as the interaction between the local and regional levels and national directorates and professional bodies

[3010] This interaction is important because several government agencies have important roles in social security work at the local and regional level

[3011] The chapter places particular emphasis on preventive social security work

[3012] The chapter also discusses the division of roles between the fire and rescue services, the police and the health service

[3013] Local and regional levels also have important roles in total defence, which are discussed in more detail in chapter

[3022] The County Governor's social security work

[3023] The County Governor is the state's representative at the regional level

[3024] The County Governor shall, in accordance with the Instructions for the County Governor's and the Governor of Svalbard's work on public safety, emergency preparedness and crisis management

[3025] Social security in an uncertain world

[3026] County Governor's social security instructions

[3027] Coordinate public safety work in the county, as well as be a driving force and guide in the work on public safety and emergency preparedness

[3028] The county governor must also be able to fulfill his responsibility for crisis management across the entire crisis spectrum from unwanted incidents in peace, security policy crises and armed conflict

[3029] The county governor's coordinating role in civil-military cooperation in the county is discussed in more detail in section

[3030] In his coordination, guidance and crisis management roles, the County Governor is dependent on having an overview of local and regional resources that are central to public safety work

[3031] Several of the county governor's activities and tasks provide broad and close contact with local and regional social security actors such as municipalities, regional agencies, businesses, and voluntary organizations

[3032] In the event of unwanted incidents, the county governor shall coordinate crisis management in the region through the county emergency management council

[3033] The council consists of representatives of regional actors responsible for critical infrastructure and critical societal functions, leaders from the police and other emergency services, the Armed Forces, the Civil Defence, voluntary organisations, the county municipality and government agencies with significant emergency response tasks in the county

[3034] The County Governor may also invite other actors

[3035] The County Governor is a key driver for coordinating social security efforts in all parts of the social security chain

[3036] Experience from the corona pandemic has made it clear how important the county governors' coordination role is during incidents, not least in contributing to a common understanding of the situation between regional and central levels

[3037] Evaluating and learning from the handling of the corona pandemic and the further development of total defense will be important work going forward

[3038] The County Governor supervises the municipalities' social security work

[3039] The audit examines, among other things, the municipalities' overview of risks and vulnerabilities and the work on prevention, preparedness and crisis management

[3040] The County Governor's supervisory responsibility includes, among other things, guiding the municipalities on how public safety under the Planning and Building Act can be ensured

[3041] As the objection authority, the county governor shall ensure that issues of public safety and the consequences of climate change of national and significant regional importance are taken into account in the municipal plan's area section and zoning plans

[3043] Municipalities have a key role in the work on social security

[3044] They have a general responsibility for ensuring the safety and security of the population within their geographical areas

[3045] Municipalities must develop safe and resilient local communities and have an important role in prevention, preparedness and crisis management

[3046] Municipalities' social security work must be comprehensive, systematic and knowledge-based
